segments.name: Vienna, the Grain Trade, and the Wrong Degree

stops.name: Vienna, born into the double kinship
stops.date_confidence: Birth date and city attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'). The exact birth address is not established in any source reached this pass; the coordinate is the canonical Vienna pin used across the atlas for the Berggasse, inherited rather than geocoded, and it does not claim to be the house he was born in.
stops.campa: He is born in Vienna in the last November of 1891, into a knot of kinship the city finds unremarkable and the century will not. His mother Anna is Sigmund Freud's sister. His father Ely is the brother of Martha Bernays, Freud's wife. The uncle is therefore an uncle twice over, once by blood and once by marriage, and the nephew will spend seventy years explaining the arithmetic to reporters who want a simpler sentence. Four of those aunts, Freud's other sisters, will die in the camps fifty-one years later, unable to get papers out of this city.
sources: freud.journey.json, the Vienna exile stops of June 1938
suggested_refs: The Freud-Bernays double marriage: Sigmund Freud to Martha Bernays, and Ely Bernays to Anna Freud

stops.name: New York, the grain floor at 2 Broadway
stops.date_confidence: The 1892 family emigration is attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'); the month is not, and is set to January to open the segment. Ely Bernays's work in the Manhattan grain trade is attested; his years on the Produce Exchange floor are not, and the coordinate is the Exchange building at 2 Broadway rather than a documented posting.
stops.campa: Ely Bernays goes ahead to the Manhattan grain trade; Anna follows with the children, and the infant becomes a New Yorker before he can walk. The Produce Exchange is the family's income and the family's expectation of him. But a second inheritance arrives in the house by letter and by conversation from Vienna, and the boy takes it in at the dinner table without ever being addressed. Children in that house were seen and not heard, he says much later. Children, he adds, listened.
stops.quote: Well I heard about my uncle's theory of dream interpretation. I heard about psychology as being an important force in evaluating human behavior. I heard of repression and regression and suppression and projection and ... taboos and oedipal complexes.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bernays, interviewed by Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers' (PBS transcript). The ellipsis marks Moyers's interjection 'Taboos?', which the commonly circulated one-sentence version of this quote silently removes.
sources: Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers', transcript at billmoyers.com
suggested_refs: The New York Produce Exchange building, 2 Broadway, Manhattan

stops.name: DeWitt Clinton High School, the largest building of its kind
stops.date_confidence: Graduation in 1908 attested (Wikipedia; Cornell CALS notable-alumni page). Month set to June by convention for a commencement. Building and address attested (Wikipedia, 'DeWitt Clinton High School'): Tenth Avenue between 58th and 59th, occupied 1906-1929. Coordinate corrected from 40.769, -73.9885, which fell about 150 m south of the block.
stops.campa: The school occupies C. B. J. Snyder's H-shaped pile on Tenth Avenue between Fifty-eighth and Fifty-ninth, said in its day to be the largest high school building in the United States, in a district of rail yards and slaughterhouses. Bernays graduates at sixteen. What he wanted to study is known only from his own accounts, written half a century afterward, and those do not agree with each other. The choice was not his to make: his father named Cornell, and named agriculture, and in the autumn of 1908 the boy goes up to Ithaca.
suggested_refs: The 1906 DeWitt Clinton building on Tenth Avenue, later Haaren High School

stops.name: Cornell, the degree he never uses
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'; Cornell CALS notable-alumni page, both fetched): an A.B. in agriculture from the College of Agriculture, taken at his father's direction. Month set to June by convention.
stops.campa: Four years on the Agricultural Quad at Ithaca produce a degree in agriculture and a young man with no intention whatever of farming. He arrives at sixteen and leaves at twenty, the youngest in most rooms and a Jewish student in a college where that is noticed and counted. He takes the degree and he takes the arrangement that comes with it: a desk at the Produce Exchange, and then a season in Paris reading cables for a grain house on the other side of an ocean.
suggested_refs: The College of Agriculture quadrangle, Cornell University, Ithaca

stops.name: Paris, the grain cables
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The stint with Louis Dreyfus & Company in Paris and the return to New York by December 1912 come from the Library of Congress biographical chronology as summarized in earlier research; no primary document was reached this pass and no office address was located. The coordinate is the canonical Paris pin and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Louis Dreyfus & Company sits him at a desk to read grain cables. He is twenty years old, in Paris, in the last summer of the world he was born into, and he is bored past bearing. Paris will hold him twice more, in December 1918 and in the spring of 1925, and both of those times as theatre rather than as trade. By December he is back in New York with no trade and no profession. A school friend named Fred Robinson has just come into two medical trade journals and needs a co-editor. He accepts.
sources: Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, biographical chronology (as summarized in earlier research; not refetched this pass)
suggested_refs: Louis Dreyfus & Company, Paris grain house, employer in 1912

segments.name: Damaged Goods: the Third Party Invented

stops.name: New York, the Medical Review of Reviews
stops.date_confidence: The co-editorship with Fred Robinson of the Medical Review of Reviews and the Dietetic and Hygienic Gazette is attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'). No editorial address was located this pass; the coordinate is a midtown Manhattan placeholder, and the month orders the segment against his December return from Paris.
stops.campa: Two small journals, a friend's inheritance, and an editorial page almost nobody reads. Bernays and Robinson print an endorsement of a French play about syphilis that no American manager will touch, and readers write in to say they agree. That is the discovery, and in sixty years of work he never really makes another. A cause will carry a product. A third party speaking for its own reasons is worth more than any quantity of paid advertising, precisely because it is not understood to be speaking for anyone.
suggested_refs: The Medical Review of Reviews and the Dietetic and Hygienic Gazette, 1912-1913

stops.name: Fulton Theatre, the Sociological Fund
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and upgraded from the earlier reconstruction: Wikipedia's article on 'Damaged Goods' names the Fulton Theatre, the first American performance on 14 March 1913 and the public premiere on 14 May, and names Bernays and the Sociological Fund directly. Coordinate corrected eastward from -73.9857 to the Fulton's site at 210 West 46th Street.
stops.campa: Richard Bennett wants to stage Eugene Brieux's Damaged Goods, a play about syphilis, in a city whose censors will close it on sight. Bernays does not fight the censors. He builds a sponsor list instead and calls it the Sociological Fund, filling it with clergymen, physicians, and philanthropists whose names no district attorney wants to prosecute, so that attendance becomes a civic duty rather than an indecency. He is twenty-one, and the method he has just assembled is the one he will still be using at ninety. The play opens at the Fulton on the fourteenth of March. Nobody is arrested.
suggested_refs: The Fulton Theatre, 210 West 46th Street, and the Sociological Fund of 1913

stops.name: Century Theatre, the Ballets Russes come to America
stops.date_confidence: Bernays's assignment to the Ballets Russes in 1915 is attested (Museum of Public Relations). The company's first American season opened in January 1916; the Century Theatre and the seventeenth as the opening day come from general accounts of that season and were not independently confirmed this pass, so venue and day are reconstruction. The old Metropolitan Opera House, given in earlier drafts, is wrong for January 1916: the Metropolitan connection is Otto Kahn's negotiation of the autumn tour.
stops.campa: Sergei Diaghilev's company is booked into America, and America does not know what ballet is. Bernays writes an eighty-one page manual for the advance agents in each city, translating the repertoire into local terms, feeding photographs to the women's pages and business stories to the trade papers, selling not the dancing but the fact that the dancing has arrived. He is twenty-four and has never seen a ballet, and a European art form has been handed to him to explain to a continent. The season opens in January 1916.
stops.quote: I was given a job about which I knew nothing.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bernays on the Ballets Russes assignment, Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
suggested_refs: Bernays's eighty-one page guide for Ballets Russes advance agents, 1915-1916

stops.name: New York harbor, Nijinsky comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: Vaslav Nijinsky's arrival in New York on 4 April 1916 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Vaslav Nijinsky'), and the pin is inherited byte-identical from vaslav_nijinsky.journey.json. Bernays's presence at the dockside rests on the Museum of Public Relations' account that he met the dancers as they landed; the particular day he was there is not documented. Earlier drafts placed Nijinsky in the 1915 assignment, which is impossible: he was interned in Austria-Hungary until the spring of 1916.
stops.campa: Vaslav Nijinsky has spent the war interned in Austria-Hungary and comes ashore in New York on the fourth of April, prised loose through diplomatic exchange. The publicist is at the pier. The greatest dancer alive is, for the purposes of the assignment, a headline that walks off a ship, and the photographs are arranged before the man has cleared customs. Bernays has still not seen the company dance. The autumn tour is negotiated separately, by Otto Kahn of the Metropolitan Opera.
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
suggested_refs: The prisoner-exchange negotiations that released Nijinsky for the 1916 American tour

stops.name: Toledo, on tour with Caruso
stops.date_confidence: A surviving photograph places Bernays and Enrico Caruso at the Shriners Temple in Toledo (Museum of Public Relations, fetched), dated there to 1917. The month and day are not established and are set to January to order the segment.
stops.campa: As publicity manager of the Metropolitan Musical Bureau he moves Enrico Caruso through the American interior, and in Toledo a photographer catches the two of them at the Shriners Temple, the tenor in a heavy coat, the young man beside him looking like somebody's clerk. Bernays is not selling music. He is selling the arrival of a famous voice in a city that has never heard one, which is a different commodity and travels better. Within months the country is at war and the same skill is requisitioned by the government.
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
suggested_refs: The 1917 photograph of Bernays and Caruso at the Shriners Temple, Toledo

stops.name: Washington, the Bureau of Latin-American Affairs
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged and not resolved: Wikipedia's timeline puts Bernays at the Committee on Public Information in 1917, while the Museum of Public Relations dates it to 1918 and Northeastern's archives record states that he joined the committee in 1918. The date here follows the two institutional sources; the month is a placeholder. The Bureau of Latin-American Affairs is named by Wikipedia; the coordinate is the committee's Washington headquarters.
stops.campa: George Creel's committee is the largest propaganda apparatus the United States has ever assembled, and it hires Bernays for the Latin American desk: American war messages placed with the business press and the newspapers of a hemisphere the fighting has not reached. He works the nationality groups as well, the Czechs and the Poles and the South Slavs who want out of the empire he was born in. In Washington the word propaganda carries no stain at all; the committee prints it in its own job titles. Whether he joined that committee in 1917 or in 1918, no two sources agree.
stops.quote: Propaganda is the executive arm of the invisible government.
stops.quote_source: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (New York: Horace Liveright, 1928), Chapter II, 'The New Propaganda'
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
suggested_refs: The CPI Bureau of Latin-American Affairs, 1917-1919

stops.name: Place de la Concorde, Wilson as godhead
stops.date_confidence: Wilson's entry into Paris on 14 December 1918 is attested. Bernays sailed with the American press mission in December 1918 and describes the reception to Bill Moyers; his own place in the crowd rests on that retrospective account alone. Earlier drafts compressed this scene into the Peace Conference, which did not open until 18 January 1919.
stops.campa: Woodrow Wilson rides in an open carriage through crowds that two years of Creel's committee have prepared to expect a deliverer, and Bernays stands in the street watching the effect of his own trade arrive in the shape of a man. What he takes from the afternoon is not a political lesson about Wilson or about peace but a technical one: the sentiment of a continent can be fastened to a single face, and it can be done deliberately, by men he could name. The conference he has sailed over for will not open for another month.
stops.quote: The effect of this activity had brought about a situation in which Woodrow Wilson became a godhead symbol.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bernays, interviewed by Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers' (PBS transcript)
sources: Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers', transcript at billmoyers.com
suggested_refs: Wilson's reception in Paris, 14 December 1918

stops.name: Quai d'Orsay, the word that angers Creel
stops.date_confidence: The Paris Peace Conference opened at the Quai d'Orsay on 18 January 1919, and Wikipedia dates Bernays's conference work to 1919. The episode of the release describing 'worldwide propaganda' and Creel's anger at it rests on Bernays's own memoir and later interviews; no contemporary document for it was reached this pass.
stops.campa: The conference opens and the American publicity group issues a release boasting of worldwide propaganda for American accomplishments. Creel is furious. In Washington the word had been a plain description of the work; printed in Paris, in front of the allied press, it becomes a confession. Bernays sails home having understood that the thing itself is not in question, only its name, and that whoever gets to name it decides what may afterward be said about it. He will spend four years looking for a phrase Americans can live with.
sources: Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers', transcript at billmoyers.com
suggested_refs: Edward L. Bernays, Biography of an Idea (1965), the Paris chapters

stops.name: New York, a title nobody has held
stops.date_confidence: The 1919 office opening and the adoption of the title 'counsel on public relations' are attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'), as is Doris Fleischman's hiring as the firm's first employee (Wikipedia, 'Doris Fleischman'). No street address was located this pass; the coordinate is a midtown Manhattan placeholder and the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He opens an office and calls himself a counsel on public relations, taking the lawyer's word on purpose, because a counsel advises and a press agent begs. The first employee is Doris Fleischman, Barnard 1913, a rewrite woman off the New York Tribune who has covered prizefights and murder trials under a masthead that would not print her name. She is the better writer of the two. For the next forty years a great deal of what the firm produces will be drafted by her and signed by him.
suggested_refs: Doris E. Fleischman's Tribune journalism, 1914-1919

stops.name: Atlanta, the NAACP conference
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction and source error flagged: the NAACP's 1920 annual conference in Atlanta is attested (New Georgia Encyclopedia) and a letter of appreciation to Bernays survives in the Museum of Public Relations catalog, which supplies the dates of 30 May to 2 June. The Wikipedia article on Bernays, cited for this in earlier drafts, contains no mention of the NAACP or Atlanta at all, and that citation is withdrawn.
stops.campa: The NAACP holds its eleventh annual conference in Atlanta, the first it has held below the line, and expects to be attacked for it. Bernays and Fleischman handle the publicity, and the meeting passes without the violence everyone had braced for; a letter of thanks goes to the office afterward. What the letter does not record is what the coverage cost. The service he sold was attention, and attention is what the branch got. The New Georgia Encyclopedia states that the publicity triggered a backlash which hurt the Atlanta branch and left most branches in the state paralyzed for the next two decades.
sources: New Georgia Encyclopedia, 'National Association for the Advancement of Colored People'
Museum of Public Relations catalog, NAACP letter of appreciation record
suggested_refs: The NAACP letter of appreciation to Bernays, June 1920

stops.name: City Hall, the marriage and the register
stops.date_confidence: The 1922 marriage and Doris Fleischman's registering at the Waldorf-Astoria under her own name are attested (Wikipedia, 'Doris Fleischman'); the exact date is not established and is set to January. City Hall as the venue is per the general biographical record: the Jewish Women's Archive page that would confirm it returned an access error when fetched this pass.
stops.campa: They marry at City Hall and go uptown to the Waldorf-Astoria, where she signs the register Doris E. Fleischman and takes the room in her own name. In 1925 she will be issued a United States passport in her birth name, reported as the first to a married American woman, and she keeps that name professionally to the end of her life; his memoir, forty-three years on, will carry mostly one of the two. Their daughters, born in 1929 and 1930, are given his. The firm's letterhead carries both names.
suggested_refs: Doris Fleischman's 1925 passport, issued in her birth name
The original Waldorf-Astoria at Fifth Avenue and 33rd Street, demolished 1929

stops.name: New York, the soap that children carve
stops.date_confidence: Procter & Gamble's hiring of Bernays and the resulting National Soap Sculpture Competition are attested (Museum of Public Relations); the year 1923 is from the same source and the month is a placeholder. The client sat in Cincinnati, but no record places Bernays there, so the stop is set at the New York office from which the campaign was run.
stops.campa: Procter & Gamble has a difficulty with Ivory: children hate washing. Bernays does not advertise the soap. He founds a national soap sculpture competition, gets it adopted into art classes and school curricula across the country, and turns a bar of Ivory into the cheapest carving stone in America. Children handle the product every week with their teachers' encouragement. The contest outlives the campaign that made it and runs on for decades after the man who invented it has moved to tobacco.
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
suggested_refs: The National Soap Sculpture Competition, Procter & Gamble, from 1924

stops.name: New York University, the first course and Crystallizing Public Opinion
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction for the teaching. Crystallizing Public Opinion is attested to 1923; the claim that Bernays taught the first university course in public relations, at New York University in the same year, rests on the Library of Congress chronology as summarized in earlier research and was not independently confirmed this pass. The Washington Square coordinate is the campus, not a located classroom, and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The book and the course arrive in the same year, and between them they do what the invented title could not do alone: they make the work a subject. Crystallizing Public Opinion argues that the counsel is an analyst of group psychology who manufactures news instead of begging for it, and that the manufacture is a technique with rules. Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion is one year old and Bernays has read it closely. Lippmann's word, the stereotype, becomes his working unit of measurement.
stops.quote: The group will cling to its stereotype, as Walter Lippmann calls it, making of those supposedly powerful beings, the leaders of public opinion, mere bits of driftwood in the surf.
stops.quote_source: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (1928), Chapter II, 'The New Propaganda'. The singular 'stereotype' is the reading of both 1928 scans; the widely circulated plural is a corruption.
sources: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (1928), read from the archive.org scan
Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, biographical chronology (as summarized in earlier research)
suggested_refs: Edward L. Bernays, Crystallizing Public Opinion (Boni and Liveright, 1923)
Walter Lippmann, Public Opinion (1922)

stops.name: The White House, the breakfast for Coolidge
stops.date_confidence: The Coolidge breakfast with Al Jolson, the Dolly Sisters and Ed Wynn is attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'; Museum of Public Relations; Bernays's own account to Moyers). The year 1924 is attested; the month and day were not established this pass and are set to January.
stops.campa: Calvin Coolidge is running for election in his own right and is famous chiefly for saying nothing. Bernays sends him vaudeville. Al Jolson comes, and the Dolly Sisters, and Ed Wynn, and they eat pancakes on the White House lawn and sing to the President, who eats with them. A campaign event has been assembled out of nothing but a guest list and a breakfast. The papers do not run it as advertising, because it is not advertising. They run it as news, under headlines of the order of 'President Nearly Laughs'.
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers', transcript at billmoyers.com
suggested_refs: Press coverage of the Coolidge breakfast, 1924

stops.name: The Louvre, American silk on the wall
stops.date_confidence: Bernays's role at the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Decoratifs, and the Cheney Brothers silks exhibited in the Louvre for the first time, are attested (Museum of Public Relations). Month set to the Exposition's April opening. The Grand Palais, named alongside the Louvre in earlier drafts, has been dropped: the Exposition grounds were a separate site and naming both made the coordinate ambiguous.
stops.campa: He has spent a year selling the Cheney Brothers silk company an idea he calls Art in Industry: that a manufactured textile is a work of art and belongs where art is hung. The 1925 Exposition gives him the room to prove it. American silks go on show in the Louvre, and the United States, which has declined to exhibit officially, is represented in Paris by a Connecticut mill and a publicist working under the title of assistant commissioner. It is, by the account that survives, the first time American manufactured goods have hung in the Louvre.
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
suggested_refs: The Cheney Brothers 'Art in Industry' campaign, from 1924
Exposition Internationale des Arts Decoratifs et Industriels Modernes, Paris 1925

stops.name: New York, the Tobacco Society for Voice Culture
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'): Bernays briefly represented Liggett & Myers, created the nominal Tobacco Society for Voice Culture against a Lucky Strike claim, and was then hired by American Tobacco's president George Washington Hill. The year is 1927; the month is a placeholder and no office address was located.
stops.campa: Lucky Strike is advertising that its cigarettes protect the throat, and Liggett & Myers, which sells Chesterfields, wants that claim stopped. Bernays invents the Tobacco Society for Voice Culture: an organization with a letterhead, a purpose, and no members, which questions the claim in public. It is the Sociological Fund again with the philanthropy taken out. Within months George Washington Hill of American Tobacco, who has watched the whole performance from the other side, hires the man who ran it against him.
suggested_refs: The Tobacco Society for Voice Culture, 1927

stops.name: New York, Propaganda
stops.date_confidence: Publication by Horace Liveright in 1928 is attested and the text was read directly from the 1928 scan on archive.org. The month is a placeholder. The coordinate is the New York office where the book was written rather than the publisher's premises.
stops.campa: He writes the argument out plainly, under the very word Creel had told him not to print. A democracy is too large for everyone's attention at once; the gap is filled by men who organize opinion; this is not a scandal but the mechanism, and the mechanism ought to be understood by the people who work it. The book sells modestly and is read closely by the wrong readers. Thirty-seven years later his memoir will report, at second hand and from a single journalist, that Goebbels kept the earlier book on a shelf in Berlin.
stops.quote: The conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses is an important element in democratic society. Those who manipulate this unseen mechanism of society constitute an invisible government which is the true ruling power of our country.
stops.quote_source: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (New York: Horace Liveright, 1928), Chapter I, 'Organizing Chaos', opening paragraph
sources: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (1928), read from the archive.org scan
Edward L. Bernays, Biography of an Idea (1965), for the Karl von Wiegand report
suggested_refs: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (Horace Liveright, 1928)

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, the torches of freedom
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Torches of Freedom'; Bernays to Moyers): Easter Sunday, 31 March 1929, in the Fifth Avenue Easter parade. The exact cross street is not established and the coordinate marks Fifth Avenue near St. Patrick's. Bernays's claim that theatre smoking rooms opened to women within five weeks is his own retrospective account and is contested; Vanessa Murphree's peer-reviewed study finds that later tellings relied on and amplified his own.
stops.campa: American Tobacco wants the half of the market that is forbidden to smoke in the street. Bernays asks the psychoanalyst A. A. Brill what a cigarette is to a woman, and Brill tells him it is a torch of freedom. So a dozen young women, one of them Bernays's own secretary Bertha Hunt, light cigarettes while walking in the Easter parade, and the newsreel men and the wire photographers have been told in advance where to stand. He will tell the story for another sixty-six years, and it will grow in the telling. Nobody prints the name of the company that paid.
stops.quote: Cigarettes are torches of freedom to women.
stops.quote_source: A. A. Brill to Bernays, as quoted by Bernays in the Bill Moyers interview 'The Image Makers'
sources: Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers', transcript at billmoyers.com
Vanessa Murphree, on the historiography of the parade story
suggested_refs: Newsreel and press coverage of the Easter parade of 31 March 1929

stops.name: Greenfield Village, Light's Golden Jubilee
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Light's Golden Jubilee'); the pin is inherited byte-identical from thomas_edison.journey.json. Scope corrected: General Electric organized the jubilee and Henry Ford then took control of it, moving the ceremony from Schenectady to Dearborn, so 'Bernays designed the event' overstates him. He is not named in the Wikipedia article at all except in a navigation template, and his documented role is the publicity design.
stops.campa: General Electric wants the fiftieth anniversary of the lamp to belong to the electrical industry, and Bernays builds the publicity around it: a radio hookup carried on as many as a hundred and forty stations, a commemorative stamp, Thomas Edison at his own reconstructed bench re-enacting the making of the filament. Herbert Hoover attends, with Marie Curie and Orville Wright; Albert Einstein speaks from Berlin by wireless. Henry Ford has taken the ceremony away from Schenectady and rebuilt Menlo Park in Michigan to hold it. The date of the lamp itself, fixed in the national calendar by this evening, is a later construction.
sources: Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, client files (as summarized in earlier research)
suggested_refs: The reconstructed Menlo Park laboratory at Greenfield Village, Dearborn, Michigan

segments.name: Beer, the Fair, and the War Loan

stops.name: New York, the brewers after Prohibition
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The United Brewers Industrial Foundation account rests on the characterization of the Library of Congress client files in earlier research; no primary document was reached this pass. The same status attaches to the report that Bernays advised Herbert Hoover late in the 1932 campaign. The month is set to December, when repeal took effect.
stops.campa: Prohibition ends and the brewers need beer to stop being a vice. Bernays sells it as a beverage of moderation, native to the American table, the drink of a temperate man rather than of a saloon. Both jobs he takes this season ask the same thing of him: take a thing the public has decided against and find it another category to live in. The other client was Herbert Hoover, whom he advised in the last weeks of the 1932 campaign. Neither engagement survives in a primary document.
sources: Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, client files (as summarized in earlier research; not refetched this pass)
suggested_refs: The United Brewers Industrial Foundation campaign, from 1933

stops.name: The Waldorf Astoria, the Green Ball
stops.date_confidence: Attested and upgraded from reconstruction: Wikipedia states that the centrepiece of the effort was 'the Green Ball, a social event at the Waldorf Astoria'. The year and month were not firmly fixed by the sources reached and the month is a placeholder. Coordinate corrected south to the Park Avenue Waldorf Astoria at 301 Park; the earlier 40.758 fell a block north.
stops.campa: The Lucky Strike package is green, women say green does not go with their clothes, and George Washington Hill will not change the package. So Bernays changes the clothes. He funds a green season: a charity Green Ball at the Waldorf Astoria, green gowns, green at the milliners, an accessories committee, art historians lecturing on green in painting, a psychologist explaining green as the colour of hope. The market moves. He has been asked to sell a cigarette and has instead adjusted what American women wear for a year.
suggested_refs: The Green Ball, Waldorf Astoria, for American Tobacco

stops.name: Flushing Meadows, the fair as an argument for democracy
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and the earlier hedge withdrawn: Wikipedia states flatly that Bernays was publicity director for the 1939 New York World's Fair. The Wikipedia article on the fair itself does not mention him. The date is the fair's opening day, 30 April 1939.
stops.campa: He is publicity director of the fair and wants it argued rather than merely sold: the World of Tomorrow, raised on an ash dump in Queens, opening in the last spring before the war. In Europe the mass rally is being run by men who have read the same literature he has and drawn the opposite conclusion from it. The following year he publishes Speak Up for Democracy, going after a line between educating a public and steering it that his own book of 1928 had felt no need to draw. Whether the line can be drawn at all, the new book does not settle.
stops.quote: Universal literacy was supposed to educate the common man to control his environment. Once he could read and write he would have a mind fit to rule. So ran the democratic doctrine. But instead of a mind, universal literacy has given him rubber stamps, rubber stamps inked with advertising slogans, with editorials, with published scientific data, with the trivialities of the tabloids and the platitudes of history, but quite innocent of original thought.
stops.quote_source: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (1928), Chapter II, 'The New Propaganda'
sources: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (1928), read from the archive.org scan
suggested_refs: Edward L. Bernays, Speak Up for Democracy (1940)

stops.name: Washington, the Third War Loan
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The wartime advisory roles with the Office of War Information, the Army and the Navy, the chairmanship of the National Advisory Committee of the Third War Loan and the co-chairmanship of the Victory Book Campaign come from the characterization of his papers in earlier research; no primary document was reached this pass. The month is set to September 1943, when the Third War Loan drive opened.
stops.campa: The war returns him to Washington in the posture of 1918, advising rather than commanding: the Office of War Information, the Army, the Navy, the National Advisory Committee of the Third War Loan, a book drive for the troops. He is fifty-one and the occupation he named has been absorbed into the machinery of the state. What he still cannot obtain, then or afterward, is the thing he wants most, which is to be treated as a scientist of the public rather than a very expensive press agent. He is back in the New York office before the surrender is signed.
sources: Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, wartime files (as summarized in earlier research; not refetched this pass)
suggested_refs: The Third War Loan drive, September 1943

stops.name: New York, the bureau for United Fruit
stops.date_confidence: Larry Tye attests the Middle America Information Bureau as one of Bernays's trademark front groups, set up for United Fruit, but gives no founding date; the year 1943 rests on the Library of Congress finding aid alone and is therefore reconstruction. No office address was located and the coordinate is a midtown Manhattan placeholder.
stops.campa: Samuel Zemurray of the United Fruit Company has taken him on, and Bernays builds the client an institution: the Middle America Information Bureau, which posts free material on the geography, nutrition and peoples of Central America to journalists, teachers and librarians. The bureau does not mention that it is the company. Larry Tye, working the archive fifty years afterward, calls it a front group. It runs until 1948, when United Fruit shuts it and keeps the man who built it.
sources: Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, United Fruit files (finding aid, as summarized in earlier research)
suggested_refs: The Middle America Information Bureau, 1943-1948

stops.name: Honolulu, the visiting professorship
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The visiting professorship at the University of Hawaii, like the return to New York University as an instructor in 1948-1950, comes from a 1951 annotated bibliography and the Library of Congress chronology as summarized in earlier research; neither was independently confirmed this pass. The month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He wants the university's authority for the field he invented and can only rent it by the semester. While he is in the Pacific the firm's largest client is a fruit company that owns a railway and the only Atlantic port in Guatemala, and that has begun to describe the government of that country as a problem. He teaches a term at Manoa, one in a series of temporary academic posts: New York University before this, Boston University long after. None of them lasts and none of them is a chair.
sources: Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, biographical chronology (as summarized in earlier research)
Annotated bibliography of Bernays, 1951 (as summarized in earlier research)

stops.name: Puerto Barrios, the two-week tour
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23): in January 1952 Bernays took the publishers of Newsweek, the Cincinnati Enquirer, the Nashville Banner and the New Orleans Item on a two-week tour of the region. Time magazine, named in earlier drafts, is not among the outlets Tye lists and has been removed. The day is not established.
stops.campa: United Fruit controls the only Atlantic seaport in the country, and Bernays brings the American press down to look at it: two weeks in January, the publishers of Newsweek, the Cincinnati Enquirer, the Nashville Banner and the New Orleans Item, walked through wharves and plantations and company hospitals by their hosts. Thomas McCann, who did publicity for the company himself, wrote afterwards that what the press would hear and see was carefully staged and regulated by the host.
sources: Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
Thomas McCann, An American Company, as quoted by Tye
suggested_refs: United Fruit's installations at Puerto Barrios, Guatemala

stops.name: New York, the memo on scientific propaganda
stops.date_confidence: The memo to United Fruit's publicity chief is quoted by Larry Tye from the Bernays papers and dated to 1952; the month is not given and is set to June to order the segment. The coordinate is the same midtown placeholder used for the bureau's office.
stops.campa: He writes to the company's publicity chief that counter-communist propaganda cannot be improvised, and that it wants the method one would bring to a plant disease. The degree he never used is in that sentence: a client that grows fruit, a political opposition handled as a blight with a known treatment. The campaign he is describing will keep placing stories about Soviet influence in Guatemala with American editors for another two years, until there is no longer a government in Guatemala to place them against.
stops.quote: This whole matter of effective counter-Communist propaganda is not one of improvising. What is needed is the same type of scientific approach that is applied, let us say, to a problem of fighting a certain plant disease.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bernays, 1952 memo to United Fruit's publicity chief, quoted in Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
sources: Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
suggested_refs: The Bernays-United Fruit correspondence, Library of Congress, Bernays Papers

stops.name: Guatemala City, the responsible correspondent
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Larry Tye, Cabinet 23): in May 1954 Bernays cited a very responsible correspondent of ours in Guatemala City on Soviet arms reaching Guatemalan communists. The pin is inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json. No document reached places Bernays himself in Guatemala; the stop marks the correspondent he kept there and the city the campaign was about, as the standing rule allows for an agent acting under the subject's direction.
stops.campa: In May he tells the client that a very responsible correspondent of theirs in Guatemala City reports Soviet arms reaching the communists. The correspondent is on the payroll. The line goes out to editors in New York and Washington as intelligence from the field, and the actual dispute, between a fruit company and a government that has expropriated its uncultivated acreage and offered the company's own tax valuation in compensation, is not the story anyone in the United States is reading.
stops.quote: to carry forward the strong aggressive tactics of the United Fruit Company in pointing the finger at Communism in Guatemala
stops.quote_source: Edward Bernays, letter to United Fruit president Kenneth H. Redmond, quoted in Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
sources: Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
suggested_refs: Bernays's Guatemala correspondence, May 1954

stops.name: Guatemala City, the fall of Arbenz
stops.date_confidence: Attested (CIA memorandum printed in the Foreign Relations of the United States, Guatemala 1952-1954, document 287, fetched): Arbenz resigned on 27 June 1954 and handed the government to the armed-forces chief Carlos Enrique Diaz, with Castillo Armas heading the resulting junta in early July. The pin is inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json. The declassified record documents PBSUCCESS independently of Bernays, and no document places him inside its command structure.
stops.campa: Jacobo Arbenz resigns on the twenty-seventh of June under bombing, invasion, and a radio station broadcasting the movements of a rebel army that does not exist. The operation belongs to the Central Intelligence Agency and was authorised the previous August. Allen Dulles runs it and John Foster Dulles handles the diplomacy, both of them lately partners of the law firm that did United Fruit's work. Bernays did not plan the coup. He had spent eleven years making certain that when it came, American editors already knew which story it was.
sources: CIA memorandum, FRUS 1952-1954, Guatemala, document 287 (history.state.gov, fetched)
Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
suggested_refs: Operation PBSUCCESS, declassified CIA and State Department records

stops.name: New York, terminated by United Fruit
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'): United Fruit terminated Bernays in 1959. The month is not established and is a placeholder. The coordinate is the same midtown placeholder used for the bureau.
stops.campa: The company lets him go after nearly twenty years. By then he has published Public Relations in 1952 and edited The Engineering of Consent in 1955, and that second phrase has become the profession's most quoted description of itself. In the memoir he has begun to write, the United Fruit work occupies a proud and entirely untroubled chapter. Guatemala under Castillo Armas is a military government, and will be at war with itself for the next thirty-six years.
sources: Larry Tye, 'Watch Out for the Top Banana', Cabinet 23 (2006)
suggested_refs: Edward L. Bernays, ed., The Engineering of Consent (University of Oklahoma Press, 1955)

stops.name: Cambridge, the office closed
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged and not resolved: Larry Tye's biography is the usual source for a move in 1962, while Wikipedia has Bernays working in New York from 1919 to 1963. The year is written here as 1963 with 1962 recorded as the competing reading, and the month is a placeholder. The coordinate is central Cambridge; no street address was established.
stops.campa: They close the New York office and move to Cambridge, meaning to retire while he writes the memoir. The retirement does not hold. A smaller practice runs out of the house for another twenty years, because the name has become an institution and clients keep arriving to hire it. Doris Fleischman, who has written a great deal of what the firm produced since 1919, is seventy-one. Whether the office shut in 1962 or 1963 the sources have never agreed, and nothing settles it.
sources: Larry Tye, The Father of Spin (1999)
suggested_refs: The Bernays house in Cambridge, Massachusetts, office of the practice after 1963

stops.name: Cambridge, Biography of an Idea
stops.date_confidence: Publication by Simon & Schuster in 1965 is attested. That the manuscript was written in Cambridge is inferential: the couple were living there, but no source reached states where it was composed, and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Eight hundred and forty-nine pages, and a settled account of what every assignment in them meant. It is the indispensable source on his career and it is also the last campaign of that career, a client engaging himself, and it was built so that every later writer on the subject would have to work through it. Doris Fleischman appears in it as a wife rather than as the author of the firm's prose, and rival practitioners appear briefly or not at all. He is seventy-three when it goes to Simon and Schuster.
suggested_refs: Edward L. Bernays, Biography of an Idea: Memoirs of Public Relations Counsel (Simon & Schuster, 1965)

stops.name: Boston University, adjunct at seventy-seven
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The adjunct professorship in Boston University's School of Public Relations, 1968-1969, comes from the Library of Congress finding aid as summarized in earlier research and was not independently confirmed this pass. The month is set to September for the start of an academic year.
stops.campa: He takes an adjunct post along the Charles and teaches students born long after the Easter parade, who will graduate into an industry of tens of thousands that did not exist when he named it. He is also, by this point, arguing that the field ought to be licensed like medicine or law, on the ground that anybody at all may call themselves what he called himself in 1919 and nobody may stop them. He tells the students the parade story. He tells everybody the parade story.
sources: Library of Congress, Edward L. Bernays Papers, finding aid (as summarized in earlier research; not refetched this pass)
suggested_refs: Boston University School of Public Relations, 1968-1969

stops.name: Cambridge, the death of Doris Fleischman
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Doris Fleischman'): death by stroke at eighty-eight. The Cambridge place of death is inferred from the couple's residence there and is not stated directly by any source reached.
stops.campa: She dies of a stroke at eighty-eight, fifty-eight years married and sixty-one years into the partnership. She had fought for her own name, carried what was reported as the first American passport issued to a married woman in her birth name, and drafted a great many of the sentences that made her husband the most quoted publicist of the century. He lives another fifteen years in the house. No second marriage and no long partnership afterward is recorded.
suggested_refs: Doris E. Fleischman, An Outline of Careers for Women (1928)

stops.name: Ithaca, the Outstanding Alumni Award
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Cornell's College of Agriculture and Life Sciences lists Bernays among its notable alumni, and the fetched page confirms that standing, but the specific Outstanding Alumni Award and the year 1985 come from earlier research and the awardees page itself was not reached this pass. The month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The college of agriculture honours the graduate who never farmed. Its public page still describes him as the father of public relations who used his expertise in psychology to manipulate public opinion, the compliment and the charge fitted into one sentence, and records his place on Life magazine's list of the hundred most influential Americans of the century. The award goes to a man who has not touched agriculture since 1912 and who put the training to professional use exactly once, in a memo to a fruit company. He is ninety-three years old, at home in Cambridge, and still taking calls from reporters.
suggested_refs: Cornell CALS Outstanding Alumni Award records

stops.name: Boston, the honorary doctorate at Northeastern
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day (Northeastern University Archives and Special Collections, subject record 2627, fetched), which also records that the university holds the Edward L. Bernays papers, collection M099, 1982-1998, bulk 1993-1995.
stops.campa: Northeastern makes him a doctor at ninety-seven and afterwards takes his papers. He has spent seventy years asking to be treated as a profession rather than a trade, and the recognition arrives at the very end in the only form the academy has to give, which is a hood and a citation read aloud. He is still working. He is still, whenever anyone asks, describing the Easter parade of 1929. The collection the university takes runs from 1982 to 1998, the bulk of it from his last three years.
sources: Northeastern University Archives and Special Collections, subject record 2627 (fetched)
suggested_refs: The Edward L. Bernays papers, collection M099, Northeastern University

stops.name: Boston, Senate Bill 374
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Bernays supported Massachusetts Senate Bill 374 in 1992, seeking registration, education, examination and ethical standards for public-relations practitioners, and that the bill failed (Museum of Public Relations). The State House coordinate marks the legislature; no record reached places him inside the building, and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: At about a hundred years old he backs a bill to license public relations in Massachusetts: registration, examination, a code, penalties for the unqualified. The argument is that a man who can put a dozen women with cigarettes on Fifth Avenue and shift a national habit ought to answer to a board, the way a physician does. It is the last public act of a hundred-year life, and it is an attempt to bind the industry he named. That industry has never wanted the licence. The bill fails.
stops.quote: It might be better to have, instead of propaganda and special pleading, committees of wise men who would choose our rulers, dictate our conduct, private and public, and decide upon the best types of clothes for us to wear and the best kinds of food for us to eat. But we have chosen the opposite method, that of open competition.
stops.quote_source: Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (1928), Chapter I, 'Organizing Chaos'
sources: Museum of Public Relations, 'Pioneer: Edward Bernays'
Edward L. Bernays, Propaganda (1928), read from the archive.org scan
suggested_refs: Massachusetts Senate Bill 374 (1992), on the registration of public relations practitioners

stops.name: Cambridge, one hundred and three
stops.date_confidence: The year, the age of 103 and death at his Cambridge home are attested (Wikipedia, 'Edward Bernays'). The exact day of 9 March and the cause, bladder cancer, come from the Washington Post obituary as cited in earlier research; the Post page returned HTTP 403 and could not be independently confirmed, so both are reconstruction. No burial place could be located in any accessible source.
stops.campa: He dies at home, having outlived by decades the argument about whether the thing he invented was compatible with the thing it served. Bill Moyers had put it to him on camera that what he was describing was not influence but power, and he had answered that he had never thought of it as power, that people want to go where they want to be led. Where he is buried is not known: Findagrave and the Post are closed to search, and Mount Auburn's own index returns nothing at all for the name.
stops.quote: Well but you see, I never thought of it as power. I never treated it as power. People want to go where they want to be led.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bernays, interviewed by Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers' (PBS transcript)
sources: Bill Moyers, 'The Image Makers', transcript at billmoyers.com
Washington Post obituary, March 1995 (cited in earlier research; HTTP 403 on refetch)
